title: Why do the wicked prosper They rise quickly. Their platforms grow.
author: Michael Foster
summary: Foster grapples with the biblical problem of theodicy: why do unethical people often prosper while the virtuous struggle? He observes that wickedness often wins in the short term because it operates without moral constraints—a wicked man will lie, steal, and betray without hesitation while a virtuous man is constrained by conscience. Foster argues that short-term advantage is not ultimate success, and that living with integrity carries rewards not measurable in money or status. He emphasizes that raising children to be virtuous even when vice appears to prosper is an act of faith—faith that integrity matters more than winning, that character is worth building even when the wicked seem to win the visible contests.
points: Wickedness often prospers in the short term because it operates without moral constraints—a wicked person will lie, steal, and betray without hesitation.
A virtuous man is constrained by conscience, which puts him at apparent disadvantage in contests where rules are ignored by the opposition.
Short-term advantage is not ultimate success—measuring life by money, status, or visible wins misses what actually constitutes a good life.
Integrity carries rewards not measurable in currency or acclaim but embodied in peace, relationships, and self-respect.
Raising children to be virtuous even when vice prospers requires faith that character matters more than winning and that integrity is worth building regardless of external outcomes.
